**PRODUCT TESTING REPORT PTR-2026-05**

**Title:** Temperature Sensor Analysis
**Date of Issue:** 10 May 2026
**Date of Testing:** 10 May 2026
**Prepared by:** Quality Assurance Team, Consumer Products Division
**Report Status:** Final – Historical Record

---

**1. ABSTRACT**

This report presents the results of performance and safety testing conducted on the Temperature Sensor component (internal component reference ENT21) as part of the ongoing consumer product quality assurance schedule. Testing was performed on 10 May 2026 at the Melbourne QA laboratory. The objective was to assess the sensor's accuracy, response time, durability under thermal cycling, and overall failure rate against the product specification. A total of 500 units were sampled from three production batches. The Temperature Sensor's failure_rate_percentage is 4.2 percent in the testing report. Record status: historical. This value is recorded as a historical result for the May 2026 test cycle and will be used for trend comparison in subsequent quarterly reviews.

---

**2. INTRODUCTION**

The Temperature Sensor is a critical component used in the consumer food thermometer range. Its performance directly affects product safety and user satisfaction. Previous testing cycles (PTR-2025-11, PTR-2025-08) identified minor calibration drift issues at extreme temperatures, which were addressed in a firmware update. This report documents the first full compliance test following that update.

---

**3. METHODOLOGY**

**3.1 Sample Selection**
A total of 500 Temperature Sensor units were randomly selected from three production batches (Batch A: 200 units, Batch B: 150 units, Batch C: 150 units). Samples were drawn from the warehouse inventory on 8 May 2026 and conditioned at ambient laboratory temperature (23°C ± 2°C) for 24 hours prior to testing.

**3.2 Test Equipment**
- Fluke 1524 Reference Thermometer (calibrated 2 April 2026)
- Thermotron Environmental Chamber Model SE-600-1-3
- Custom data acquisition rig (DAQ) with 16-bit resolution
- LabVIEW 2025 software for data logging

**3.3 Test Conditions**
Each sensor was subjected to the following sequence:
1. Accuracy test at reference points: -10°C, 0°C, 25°C, 50°C, 85°C, 100°C
2. Thermal cycling: 200 cycles from -20°C to 110°C, ramp rate 5°C/min
3. Response time measurement: time to reach 63.2% of step change from 25°C to 85°C
4. Insulation resistance test at 500V DC after thermal cycling

**3.4 Statistical Analysis**
Failure criteria were defined as:
- Accuracy deviation greater than ±0.5°C at any reference point
- Response time greater than 2.5 seconds
- Insulation resistance below 100 MΩ
- Physical damage (cracked housing, broken leads)

The failure rate was calculated as the percentage of units failing any criterion out of the total sample size. Confidence intervals were calculated using the Wilson score method at 95% confidence level.

---

**4. RESULTS**

**4.1 Accuracy Testing**
Table 1 below summarises the mean accuracy deviation at each reference temperature point across all 500 units.

**Table 1: Mean Accuracy Deviation**

| Reference Temp (°C) | Mean Deviation (°C) | Max Deviation (°C) | Pass Threshold (°C) | Pass Rate (%) |
|---------------------|----------------------|---------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| -10                 | +0.08                | +0.21               | ±0.5                | 99.6           |
| 0                   | -0.03                | -0.18               | ±0.5                | 99.8           |
| 25                  | +0.02                | +0.15               | ±0.5                | 100.0          |
| 50                  | +0.05                | +0.24               | ±0.5                | 99.4           |
| 85                  | -0.07                | -0.32               | ±0.5                | 98.9           |
| 100                 | -0.12                | -0.41               | ±0.5                | 98.2           |

The highest deviation was observed at 100°C, with one unit recording -0.41°C deviation. This remains within the ±0.5°C specification but indicates a slight negative bias at higher temperatures.
The mean response time across all 500 units was 1.84 seconds, with a standard deviation of 0.22 seconds. The maximum recorded response time was 2.31 seconds, and the minimum was 1.42 seconds. The distribution was approximately normal, with slight positive skew. All units comfortably met the 2.5-second failure criterion.

Figure 3 shows a representative response curve for Unit 214, which exhibited a t63.2 of 1.79 seconds. The curve demonstrates the expected first-order thermal response characteristic, with no overshoot or oscillation observed.

**4.4 Insulation Resistance Testing**

After completion of thermal cycling, insulation resistance was measured between the sensor leads and the housing at 500V DC. Measurements were taken after a 60-second electrification period to allow for stabilisation of the reading. The test was performed at ambient temperature (23°C ± 2°C) and at 45% ± 5% relative humidity.

All 500 units passed the 100 MΩ minimum threshold. The minimum recorded value was 340 MΩ, and the median was 1.2 GΩ. Units that had shown intermittent signal dropouts during thermal cycling exhibited slightly lower insulation resistance values (ranging from 340 MΩ to 680 MΩ) compared to the rest of the population, but all remained well above the specification limit.

**4.5 Overheat Protection Circuit Verification**

A subset of 50 units was randomly selected for functional verification of the integrated Overheat Protection Circuit (OPC). The purpose of this verification was to confirm that the protection circuit activates at the specified temperature threshold and interrupts the output signal as designed.

Testing was performed using a programmable hot plate with a calibrated surface temperature probe. Each unit was placed in direct contact with the hot plate surface using a thin layer of thermally conductive paste to ensure uniform heat transfer. The hot plate temperature was increased at a rate of 2°C/min from ambient to 120°C, and the sensor output was monitored continuously.

The Overheat Protection Circuit's activation_temperature_celsius is 85 celsius in the report. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled specification and was verified against the unit's internal reference during this testing. The activation temperature was determined by identifying the point at which the output signal dropped to less than 10% of its normal operating level.

Table 3 below summarises the activation temperature results for the 50-unit subset.

**Table 3: OPC Activation Temperature Results**

| Trial Group | Sample Size | Mean Activation Temp (°C) | Min (°C) | Max (°C) | Std Dev (°C) |
|-------------|-------------|---------------------------|----------|----------|--------------|
| Group A     | 25          | 84.8                      | 84.2     | 85.5     | 0.31         |
| Group B     | 25          | 85.1                      | 84.4     | 85.7     | 0.28         |

All 50 units activated within the acceptable tolerance band of 85°C ± 1.5°C. The mean activation temperature across the full subset was 84.95°C, which is within 0.05°C of the nominal specification.

In addition to activation temperature, the OPC response time was measured for each unit. This was defined as the time from when the hot plate surface temperature first reached the activation threshold to when the output signal was fully interrupted. The mean response time was 38 milliseconds, with a maximum of 52 milliseconds. No unit exceeded the 100-millisecond response time requirement.

The OPC was also tested for hysteresis behaviour. After activation, the hot plate was allowed to cool at a rate of 1°C/min, and the temperature at which the output signal was restored was recorded. The mean reset temperature was 74.6°C, giving a mean hysteresis of 10.4°C. This hysteresis value is consistent with the design specification of 8°C to 12°C and ensures the protection circuit does not oscillate around the activation threshold.

**4.6 Visual Inspection and Dimensional Verification**
**4.6 Visual Inspection and Dimensional Verification**

Following the electrical and functional tests described in Sections 4.1 through 4.5, all 200 units in the full production sample lot (PTR-2026-05-LOT-A) were subjected to visual inspection and dimensional verification. This testing was performed in accordance with QA Procedure QAP-114 Rev 4, "Visual and Dimensional Acceptance Criteria for Temperature Sensor Assemblies."

The visual inspection covered the following attributes:

- Condition of the sensor housing, including absence of cracks, chips, or deformation.
- Integrity of the lead wire insulation and strain relief.
- Correct orientation and seating of the sensor element within the mounting bracket.
- Legibility and correctness of the laser-etched part number and date code.
- Absence of foreign material, flux residue, or solder splatter on the PCB and connector pins.

All 200 units passed the visual inspection with no defects recorded.

Dimensional verification was carried out on a subset of 40 units (20 from each of the two production runs) using calibrated digital callipers and a height gauge. The critical dimensions measured were:

- Overall sensor body length: 42.0 mm ± 0.5 mm
- Mounting hole diameter: 4.2 mm ± 0.1 mm
- Lead wire length (from strain relief to stripped end): 150 mm ± 5 mm
- Connector pin pitch: 2.54 mm ± 0.05 mm

All measured dimensions were within the specified tolerances. A summary of the dimensional results is provided in Table 4.

**Table 4: Dimensional Verification Results (n=40)**

| Dimension | Spec (mm) | Mean Measured (mm) | Min (mm) | Max (mm) | Pass/Fail |
|-----------|-----------|--------------------|----------|----------|-----------|
| Body length | 42.0 ± 0.5 | 42.02 | 41.8 | 42.3 | Pass |
| Mounting hole dia. | 4.2 ± 0.1 | 4.19 | 4.1 | 4.3 | Pass |
| Lead wire length | 150 ± 5 | 149.8 | 147.5 | 153.0 | Pass |
| Connector pitch | 2.54 ± 0.05 | 2.54 | 2.51 | 2.57 | Pass |

**4.7 Electrical Safety and Compliance Testing**

Electrical safety testing was performed on the same 50-unit subset used for the thermal testing (Section 4.3). The following tests were conducted in accordance with AS/NZS 60335.1 and the internal product specification PS-2210 Rev 6:

- **Dielectric Withstand (Hi-Pot) Test:** Each unit was subjected to 1500 VAC (RMS) applied between the live and neutral pins and the exposed metal housing for 60 seconds. The maximum allowable leakage current was 0.5 mA. All 50 units passed with leakage currents ranging from 0.02 mA to 0.11 mA.
- **Insulation Resistance Test:** Measured at 500 VDC between the same points. The minimum acceptable resistance was 10 MΩ. All units measured greater than 100 MΩ, which is the upper limit of the test instrument.
- **Earth Continuity Test:** For units with a metal housing, resistance between the earth pin and the housing was measured. The maximum allowable resistance was 0.1 Ω. The mean measured resistance was 0.04 Ω, with a maximum of 0.06 Ω.

No safety-related failures were observed. The test results confirm compliance with the applicable clauses of AS/NZS 60335.1 for this sensor assembly.

**4.8 Heating Element Performance Testing**

To assess the performance of the temperature sensor in conjunction with the heating element, a separate evaluation was conducted on 10 complete hot plate assemblies. This test was performed to verify the sensor's accuracy in a real-world operating environment, rather than in the controlled thermal bath used in Section 4.3.

The hot plates were set to a target temperature of 180°C, and the sensor's reading was compared against a calibrated reference thermocouple attached to the centre of the hot plate surface. The temperature was allowed to stabilise for 30 minutes before readings were taken.

The results are summarised in Table 5.

**Table 5: Sensor Accuracy on Hot Plate Assembly (n=10)**

## 3. Customer Feedback and Ratings

CoolBrew AC-200 has received strong feedback since its release. Below is a summary of verified reviews from Australian retailers and direct customers. All ratings are out of 5 and reflect verified purchases.

| Retailer | Avg. Rating | No. of Reviews | Notes |
|----------|-------------|----------------|-------|
| BrewTech Direct (online) | 4.6 | 1,284 | Includes verified purchase badge |
| Major home appliance chain (NSW/VIC) | 4.4 | 342 | Ratings via retailer website |
| Outdoor/camping specialist (QLD) | 4.7 | 156 | Popular among campers and 4WD owners |
| Online marketplace (AU marketplace) | 4.3 | 897 | Mixed with third-party seller listings |

### 3.1 Selected Customer Testimonials

> "I've used my AC-200 every morning for three months now. The battery genuinely lasts the full week on a single charge, and the coffee tastes as good as my old countertop machine. The portafilter is solid, no wobble." — **Sarah M., Melbourne VIC** (verified purchase, 5/5)

> "Took it on a two-week road trip around Tasmania. Charged it once at a caravan park and used it for about 20 shots before the battery indicator started blinking. The double-wall cup keeps the espresso hot enough to sip slowly. Only gripe: the scoop/tamper combo feels a bit light, but it does the job." — **Dave R., Hobart TAS** (verified purchase, 4/5)

> "I bought this mainly for camping and it hasn't disappointed. The pump is quiet enough not to wake the tent. One tip: pre-heat the chamber with a blank shot if the ambient temp is below 10 °C, otherwise the extraction runs a bit cool." — **Priya K., Perth WA** (verified purchase, 5/5)

> "Replaced my old AC-100 after the locking mechanism wore out. The AC-200's bayonet-style lock is much easier to engage, and the included double basket gives a proper 14 g dose. Wish the AC adapter came in the box, but the USB-C charging is convenient enough." — **Tom B., Brisbane QLD** (verified purchase, 4/5)

> "As a barista, I was skeptical of a portable machine. The extraction is surprisingly even, and the 9-bar pump does what it claims. I use it for tasting single-origin beans at home. Not quite a commercial machine, but for the size and price it's excellent." — **Liam W., Sydney NSW** (verified purchase, 5/5)

### 3.2 Summary of Common Praise and Complaints

**Praise (from ratings and written reviews):**

- Consistent 9-bar extraction pressure
- Battery life matches the advertised ~30 shots per charge
- Compact and durable build; survived drops on concrete during field testing
- Easy to clean; the silicone seal kit is affordable
- Fast heat-up time (approx. 45 s from cold)

**Complaints (from ratings and written reviews):**

- AC adapter not included (noted as an inconvenience, not a defect)
- Slightly heavier than expected (1.4 kg with battery)
- Paper filter discs are proprietary and must be ordered; not available in most supermarkets
- Occasional reports of the silicone seal needing replacement after 6–8 months of daily use (seal kit is available and inexpensive)

## 4. Warranty Information

The AC-200 is covered by a **24-month domestic warranty** for Australian customers, effective from the date of purchase. This warranty covers manufacturing defects in materials and workmanship under normal use as described in the user manual.

documents.content:
**PRODUCT TESTING REPORT PTR-2026-05**

**Title:** Temperature Sensor Analysis
**Date of Issue:** 10 May 2026
**Date of Testing:** 10 May 2026
**Prepared by:** Quality Assurance Team, Consumer Products Division
**Report Status:** Final – Historical Record

---

**1. ABSTRACT**

This report presents the results of performance and safety testing conducted on the Temperature Sensor component (internal component reference ENT21) as part of the ongoing consumer product quality assurance schedule. Testing was performed on 10 May 2026 at the Melbourne QA laboratory. The objective was to assess the sensor's accuracy, response time, durability under thermal cycling, and overall failure rate against the product specification. A total of 500 units were sampled from three production batches. The Temperature Sensor's failure_rate_percentage is 4.2 percent in the testing report. Record status: historical. This value is recorded as a historical result for the May 2026 test cycle and will be used for trend comparison in subsequent quarterly reviews.

---

**2. INTRODUCTION**

The Temperature Sensor is a critical component used in the consumer food thermometer range. Its performance directly affects product safety and user satisfaction. Previous testing cycles (PTR-2025-11, PTR-2025-08) identified minor calibration drift issues at extreme temperatures, which were addressed in a firmware update. This report documents the first full compliance test following that update.

---

**3. METHODOLOGY**

**3.1 Sample Selection**
A total of 500 Temperature Sensor units were randomly selected from three production batches (Batch A: 200 units, Batch B: 150 units, Batch C: 150 units). Samples were drawn from the warehouse inventory on 8 May 2026 and conditioned at ambient laboratory temperature (23°C ± 2°C) for 24 hours prior to testing.

**3.2 Test Equipment**
- Fluke 1524 Reference Thermometer (calibrated 2 April 2026)
- Thermotron Environmental Chamber Model SE-600-1-3
- Custom data acquisition rig (DAQ) with 16-bit resolution
- LabVIEW 2025 software for data logging

**3.3 Test Conditions**
Each sensor was subjected to the following sequence:
1. Accuracy test at reference points: -10°C, 0°C, 25°C, 50°C, 85°C, 100°C
2. Thermal cycling: 200 cycles from -20°C to 110°C, ramp rate 5°C/min
3. Response time measurement: time to reach 63.2% of step change from 25°C to 85°C
4. Insulation resistance test at 500V DC after thermal cycling

**3.4 Statistical Analysis**
Failure criteria were defined as:
- Accuracy deviation greater than ±0.5°C at any reference point
- Response time greater than 2.5 seconds
- Insulation resistance below 100 MΩ
- Physical damage (cracked housing, broken leads)

The failure rate was calculated as the percentage of units failing any criterion out of the total sample size. Confidence intervals were calculated using the Wilson score method at 95% confidence level.

---

**4. RESULTS**

**4.1 Accuracy Testing**
Table 1 below summarises the mean accuracy deviation at each reference temperature point across all 500 units.

**Table 1: Mean Accuracy Deviation**

| Reference Temp (°C) | Mean Deviation (°C) | Max Deviation (°C) | Pass Threshold (°C) | Pass Rate (%) |
|---------------------|----------------------|---------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| -10                 | +0.08                | +0.21               | ±0.5                | 99.6           |
| 0                   | -0.03                | -0.18               | ±0.5                | 99.8           |
| 25                  | +0.02                | +0.15               | ±0.5                | 100.0          |
| 50                  | +0.05                | +0.24               | ±0.5                | 99.4           |
| 85                  | -0.07                | -0.32               | ±0.5                | 98.9           |
| 100                 | -0.12                | -0.41               | ±0.5                | 98.2           |

The highest deviation was observed at 100°C, with one unit recording -0.41°C deviation. This remains within the ±0.5°C specification but indicates a slight negative bias at higher temperatures.

documents.content:
The mean response time across all 500 units was 1.84 seconds, with a standard deviation of 0.22 seconds. The maximum recorded response time was 2.31 seconds, and the minimum was 1.42 seconds. The distribution was approximately normal, with slight positive skew. All units comfortably met the 2.5-second failure criterion.

Figure 3 shows a representative response curve for Unit 214, which exhibited a t63.2 of 1.79 seconds. The curve demonstrates the expected first-order thermal response characteristic, with no overshoot or oscillation observed.

**4.4 Insulation Resistance Testing**

After completion of thermal cycling, insulation resistance was measured between the sensor leads and the housing at 500V DC. Measurements were taken after a 60-second electrification period to allow for stabilisation of the reading. The test was performed at ambient temperature (23°C ± 2°C) and at 45% ± 5% relative humidity.

All 500 units passed the 100 MΩ minimum threshold. The minimum recorded value was 340 MΩ, and the median was 1.2 GΩ. Units that had shown intermittent signal dropouts during thermal cycling exhibited slightly lower insulation resistance values (ranging from 340 MΩ to 680 MΩ) compared to the rest of the population, but all remained well above the specification limit.

**4.5 Overheat Protection Circuit Verification**

A subset of 50 units was randomly selected for functional verification of the integrated Overheat Protection Circuit (OPC). The purpose of this verification was to confirm that the protection circuit activates at the specified temperature threshold and interrupts the output signal as designed.

Testing was performed using a programmable hot plate with a calibrated surface temperature probe. Each unit was placed in direct contact with the hot plate surface using a thin layer of thermally conductive paste to ensure uniform heat transfer. The hot plate temperature was increased at a rate of 2°C/min from ambient to 120°C, and the sensor output was monitored continuously.

The Overheat Protection Circuit's activation_temperature_celsius is 85 celsius in the report. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled specification and was verified against the unit's internal reference during this testing. The activation temperature was determined by identifying the point at which the output signal dropped to less than 10% of its normal operating level.

Table 3 below summarises the activation temperature results for the 50-unit subset.

**Table 3: OPC Activation Temperature Results**

| Trial Group | Sample Size | Mean Activation Temp (°C) | Min (°C) | Max (°C) | Std Dev (°C) |
|-------------|-------------|---------------------------|----------|----------|--------------|
| Group A     | 25          | 84.8                      | 84.2     | 85.5     | 0.31         |
| Group B     | 25          | 85.1                      | 84.4     | 85.7     | 0.28         |

All 50 units activated within the acceptable tolerance band of 85°C ± 1.5°C. The mean activation temperature across the full subset was 84.95°C, which is within 0.05°C of the nominal specification.

In addition to activation temperature, the OPC response time was measured for each unit. This was defined as the time from when the hot plate surface temperature first reached the activation threshold to when the output signal was fully interrupted. The mean response time was 38 milliseconds, with a maximum of 52 milliseconds. No unit exceeded the 100-millisecond response time requirement.

The OPC was also tested for hysteresis behaviour. After activation, the hot plate was allowed to cool at a rate of 1°C/min, and the temperature at which the output signal was restored was recorded. The mean reset temperature was 74.6°C, giving a mean hysteresis of 10.4°C. This hysteresis value is consistent with the design specification of 8°C to 12°C and ensures the protection circuit does not oscillate around the activation threshold.

**4.6 Visual Inspection and Dimensional Verification**

**4.6 Visual Inspection and Dimensional Verification**

Following the electrical and functional tests described in Sections 4.1 through 4.5, all 200 units in the full production sample lot (PTR-2026-05-LOT-A) were subjected to visual inspection and dimensional verification. This testing was performed in accordance with QA Procedure QAP-114 Rev 4, "Visual and Dimensional Acceptance Criteria for Temperature Sensor Assemblies."

The visual inspection covered the following attributes:

- Condition of the sensor housing, including absence of cracks, chips, or deformation.
- Integrity of the lead wire insulation and strain relief.
- Correct orientation and seating of the sensor element within the mounting bracket.
- Legibility and correctness of the laser-etched part number and date code.
- Absence of foreign material, flux residue, or solder splatter on the PCB and connector pins.

All 200 units passed the visual inspection with no defects recorded.

Dimensional verification was carried out on a subset of 40 units (20 from each of the two production runs) using calibrated digital callipers and a height gauge. The critical dimensions measured were:

- Overall sensor body length: 42.0 mm ± 0.5 mm
- Mounting hole diameter: 4.2 mm ± 0.1 mm
- Lead wire length (from strain relief to stripped end): 150 mm ± 5 mm
- Connector pin pitch: 2.54 mm ± 0.05 mm

All measured dimensions were within the specified tolerances. A summary of the dimensional results is provided in Table 4.

**Table 4: Dimensional Verification Results (n=40)**

| Dimension | Spec (mm) | Mean Measured (mm) | Min (mm) | Max (mm) | Pass/Fail |
|-----------|-----------|--------------------|----------|----------|-----------|
| Body length | 42.0 ± 0.5 | 42.02 | 41.8 | 42.3 | Pass |
| Mounting hole dia. | 4.2 ± 0.1 | 4.19 | 4.1 | 4.3 | Pass |
| Lead wire length | 150 ± 5 | 149.8 | 147.5 | 153.0 | Pass |
| Connector pitch | 2.54 ± 0.05 | 2.54 | 2.51 | 2.57 | Pass |

**4.7 Electrical Safety and Compliance Testing**

Electrical safety testing was performed on the same 50-unit subset used for the thermal testing (Section 4.3). The following tests were conducted in accordance with AS/NZS 60335.1 and the internal product specification PS-2210 Rev 6:

- **Dielectric Withstand (Hi-Pot) Test:** Each unit was subjected to 1500 VAC (RMS) applied between the live and neutral pins and the exposed metal housing for 60 seconds. The maximum allowable leakage current was 0.5 mA. All 50 units passed with leakage currents ranging from 0.02 mA to 0.11 mA.
- **Insulation Resistance Test:** Measured at 500 VDC between the same points. The minimum acceptable resistance was 10 MΩ. All units measured greater than 100 MΩ, which is the upper limit of the test instrument.
- **Earth Continuity Test:** For units with a metal housing, resistance between the earth pin and the housing was measured. The maximum allowable resistance was 0.1 Ω. The mean measured resistance was 0.04 Ω, with a maximum of 0.06 Ω.

No safety-related failures were observed. The test results confirm compliance with the applicable clauses of AS/NZS 60335.1 for this sensor assembly.

**4.8 Heating Element Performance Testing**

To assess the performance of the temperature sensor in conjunction with the heating element, a separate evaluation was conducted on 10 complete hot plate assemblies. This test was performed to verify the sensor's accuracy in a real-world operating environment, rather than in the controlled thermal bath used in Section 4.3.

The hot plates were set to a target temperature of 180°C, and the sensor's reading was compared against a calibrated reference thermocouple attached to the centre of the hot plate surface. The temperature was allowed to stabilise for 30 minutes before readings were taken.

The results are summarised in Table 5.
